extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed inventions integrate judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) into a practical application under the Alice/Mayo two-step framework (Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recites significantly more than a judicial exception (Step 2B), consider whether the additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words "apply it" (or an equivalent). The additional element or combination of elements must do "more than simply stat[e] the [judicial exception] while adding the words 'apply it'".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that amount to nothing more than an instruction to apply the abstract idea or other exception using a generic computer do not render the abstract idea eligible (see Alice, Mayo, Benson). Examiners should explain on the record why additional elements do not meaningfully limit the judicial exception when appropriate. This consideration often overlaps with other considerations (improvement, particular machine, particular transformation, well-understood routine/conventional) and examiners should evaluate all relevant considerations before determining whether an element is more than mere instructions. Note: the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration is evaluated in Step 2B and should not be used in Step 2A Prong Two analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciting only the idea of a solution or outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., the claim fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished). Recitations that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism are equivalent to the words "apply it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-oriented or purely functional claims that lack specific steps or mechanisms are likely mere instructions to apply the judicial exception. Examples include claims that only describe creating or modifying documents (e.g., dynamic XML modifications) without describing how the computer performs the modifications (Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One; Electric Power Group). Claiming a particular solution or way to achieve the outcome may integrate the exception into a practical application; mere result-focused language cautioned against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoking computers or other machinery merely as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process (i.e., use in its ordinary capacity for tasks such as receive, store, or transmit data), or simply adds a general-purpose computer or components after the fact to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of generic computer components or machinery in their ordinary capacity (e.g., telephone unit, server, cell phone) does not integrate a judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV; TLI Communications). In contrast, claims that improve computer capabilities or an existing technology may integrate the exception (McRO; Enfish). See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a) for further discussion of improvements to computer functioning or other technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity versus generality of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception: broadly applicable claims across many fields may not provide meaningful limitations that integrate the exception into a practical application; a claim that generically recites an effect or every mode of accomplishing an effect amounts to merely adding 'apply it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that confine the judicial exception to a particular, practical application may amount to significantly more (e.g., BASCOM: installation of a filtering tool at a specific location with customizable features). Historical cases (O'Reilly v. Morse; The Telephone Cases) show claims that attempt to monopolize a law or effect across all means are ineligible. Evaluate whether the limitation confines the abstract idea to a specific technological implementation or environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of overlapping factors (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional)
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, examiners may evaluate other related considerations (improvement to technology, particular machine, particular transformation, and well-understood/routine/conventional) to assist in determining whether an element is more than mere instructions to apply an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These considerations often overlap with the 'mere instructions' analysis and may be informative. However, the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration should not be evaluated in the Step 2A Prong Two analysis because it is reserved for Step 2B. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(a) (improvement), 2106.05(b)/(c) (particular machine/transformation), and 2106.05(d) (well-understood/routine/conventional) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception. 'Extra-solution activity' are activities incidental to the primary process or product that are merely nominal or tangential additions (includes pre-solution and post-solution activity). The addition of insignificant extra-solution activity does not amount to an inventive concept, particularly when well-understood or conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of pre-solution activity: data-gathering steps (e.g., obtaining credit card transaction info for fraud analysis). Examples of post-solution activity: printing a report. Supreme Court precedent (Flook, Mayo) holds that post-solution or merely conventional activity cannot transform an unpatentable principle into a patentable process. Examiners should carefully consider each claim on its merits and explain why such elements do not meaningfully limit the claim. Evaluation of particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, and field-of-use/technological-environment considerations may assist in the determination, but the well-understood/routine/conventional consideration is evaluated in Step 2B, not in Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the extra-solution limitation is well-known
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the extra-solution limitation is well-known such that it is token or nominal extra-solution activity (e.g., well-known random analysis techniques, known XML tags, conventional data-gathering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Token or well-known activities have been found to be insufficient to supply an inventive concept (Bilski; Flook; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.). Because this overlaps with the well-understood/routine/conventional consideration, it should not be considered in Step 2A Prong Two analysis (it is part of Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation imposes meaningful limits (significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the limitation is significant — i.e., it imposes meaningful limits on the claim so that it is not merely nominal or tangentially related to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations that meaningfully restrict the scope of the claim may be treated as adding significantly more and are considered in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examples where limitations were found insignificant include restricting public access to media (Ultramercial) and certain electronic menu ordering features (Ameranth). Provide explanation in eligibility rejections about why a limitation is not significant when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the limitation is merely necessary data gathering or outputting that all uses of the recited judicial exception would require (e.g., measuring metabolites, presenting offers and gathering statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such necessary data-gathering/output steps have been treated as insignificant extra-solution activity (Mayo; OIP Technologies). This consideration is relevant in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B analyses. Examiners should explain why such data-gathering/output steps do or do not meaningfully limit the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of Insignificant Extra-Solution Activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete categories and examples the courts have found to be insignificant extra-solution activity: (a) Mere data gathering (performing clinical tests, testing systems for responses, presenting offers and gathering statistics, obtaining transaction info, consulting/updating logs, determining biomarker levels); (b) Selecting a particular data source or type (limiting a database index to XML tags, taking certain types of food orders, selecting info in power-grid environment, requiring user request to view advertisement); (c) Insignificant application (cutting hair after determining style; printing/downloading menus); (d) Insignificant computer implementation (using conventional computers/implementation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These illustrative examples (with cited cases: In re Grams; In re Meyers; OIP Technologies; CyberSource; Ultramercial; Mayo; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.; Ameranth; Electric Power Group; In re Brown; Fort Properties; Bancorp; etc.) help identify extra-solution activities that are nominal and do not add an inventive concept. Examiners should explain why such activities do not meaningfully limit the claim when making an eligibility rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of Use and Technological Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional elements amount to more than generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Merely indicating a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception does not amount to significantly more than the exception itself and cannot integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court precedent (Diamond v. Diehr; Parker v. Flook) and Federal Circuit decisions emphasize that limiting an abstract idea to a particular field of use or adding token post-solution components does not make the concept patentable (Bilski citing Flook). Examiners should not accept mere field-of-use limitations as supplying significantly more; instead assess whether the limitation meaningfully confines the exception to a practical implementation.
